playbook:
My job in this game is to maximize declared cash plus deed values at the end, so my working rule is: buying is free on net worth — spending cash on a deed converts, never loses — the only real cost is liquidity going to zero.

- When I land on an unowned property and have at least the price in cash, I buy it. The deed counts at face value toward my final score, so there is no downside except losing rent-paying liquidity, and the deed pays rent that offsetting.
- When my cash after purchase would be very low, I still buy, because even a single rent collection from a rival recovers more than the risk of sitting cash-poor with another player's property to hit.
- When the price exceeds my cash, I declare [buy: no]; I never pretend I can afford it. (On the last lap I wrongly said I'll buy and then declared no — next time I keep my reasoning and my tokens in agreement.)
- When I land on my own property, I pay nothing and buy nothing; I just re-declare my unchanged balance.
- When I pass START, I remember to add the salary into my balance before declaring — the balance token must include it, as I did when going from 4 to 39 (4 + 25 + 10 rent).
- When I receive rent between turns, I fold it into the new balance immediately; my last declared balance is stale until I add "since your last turn you received X."
- When deciding between buying and holding cash, I check rents of what I'd be landing on: cheap high-rent properties (rent/price ratio near 0.2+) are my priority purchases; I prefer those over cash hoarding at almost any liquidity level.
- When late in the game a property is too expensive to afford, I don't worry about it — one turn can't happen again, so the lost purchase matters less than accurate bookkeeping.
- Every turn I reply exactly with the three tokens, balance computed as: prior balance + salary if passed START + rent received since last turn − purchases. I never declare a number I can't trace to that ledger.

1.text:
- My score is declared cash plus the purchase price of my deeds, so a purchase converts cash into an equal amount of score-bearing property while also letting me collect future rent and denying it to rivals. When an unowned tile is put to me and I can afford it, I buy: there is no downside unless a known future rent payment would force me below zero.
- When I cannot afford a tile, I still check whether the next expected rent I owe minus upcoming salary would sink me; only then do I pass, and I keep the arithmetic in my declaration.
- I track every rival purchase off the bank's book; before my roll of each turn I note whose deed I could land on and confirm I hold enough cash to cover the worst rent until my next salary.
- When I land on a rival's tile, I pay the exact listed rent, recompute my balance immediately, and declare it — I never let the balance drift from my own book.
- When I pass or land on START, I add the salary before declaring, since under-declaring costs me score and over-declaring risks exposure.
- When the last lap opens on an unowned tile, I buy without hesitation even if it nearly empties my cash — cash and deed price score identically, and the deed removes the tile from rivals.
- My declarations drive the ledger, so I keep every number exact and always end with the balance token; a sloppy declaration is a free loss.
- What did not work was drifting through early laps without a plan while a single rival swept every cheap deed in front of me; I commit to claiming whatever tile I can reach as early as possible so the circuit starts paying me instead of draining me.

2.text:
## My ref_estate playbook

**Core accounting discipline**
- I always recompute my balance from scratch each turn: last balance + salary (if I passed START) − rent paid − purchase price. I never trust memory alone; I recount before declaring [balance: N], since a wrong declaration is a self-inflicted wound.
- I check the "last declared balance" line and the prompt's salary flag before writing anything. If I passed START, I add 25 even on the lap I cross it.
- I only declare [pay: N to Pk] when the prompt explicitly names an owner and a rent figure. Landing on my own deed, START, or an unowned tile means [pay: none].
- I never offer [buy: yes] on a tile already owned — it's invalid and wastes nothing but signals sloppiness.

**Buying rule: deeds are nearly free money**
- Buying converts cash 1:1 into deed value, so my net worth never drops from a purchase itself. Buying is therefore almost always correct in net-worth terms; the only real cost is rent-risk from holding less cash.
- Default position: if a tile is unowned and I can afford it, I buy it — unless doing so would leave me unable to cover a likely rent hit within my remaining turns.
- I keep a liquidity cushion: before buying, I estimate the worst rent I could owe before my next salary (roughly the opponents' highest rent) and decline only if the purchase leaves me below that cushion. Passing on a cheap deed out of pure caution is a mistake I won't repeat — a skipped unowned tile is value another investor may grab later.
- Tiles I skipped earlier: if they stay unowned and lap back around to me, I buy them on the second pass with cash from salary.

**Endgame rule**
- On the final lap, cash and deeds count identically and there is no future rent to fear. I buy every unowned tile I can afford, emptying my wallet if necessary — there's zero downside.

**Salience checks each turn**
- I scan the recent-transfers log to know who owns what, so I can anticipate rent I'll owe on my next roll and size my cushion accordingly.
- I note the rents of opponents' deeds: if I'm due to land near high-rent tiles (Exchange-class, 24–30), my cushion floor is that rent; near low-rent tiles I can buy more aggressively.

**Format discipline**
- I keep reasoning to two or three sentences and always end the reply with the three bracketed tokens, on their own lines, exactly as specified: [pay: ...] (or [pay: none]), [buy: yes/no], [balance: N]. One cluster of tokens on a single line risks a parse failure; separate lines every time.

**What I will not do again**
- I will not pass on a mid-priced deed purely because it zeroes my cash early in the game when salary and rent income are still coming — lost deed value at game end costs more than a small transcript of caution. I'll formalize the cushion rule instead of going by gut feel.
- I will not compress the tokens onto one line; clean formatting is free insurance.
